passage: Zeenat, you asked how I got the scooter so cheap. Okay, so. The seller in Kothrud said, "Sixty thousand, fixed." And my brain went, oh, sixty, so fifty-five would be a steal. I actually opened my mouth to say fifty-five. Then I stopped and asked myself: if he had never said sixty, what would I think this scooter is worth? Honestly, I had no idea. So I said I'd come back. That night I found three listings for the same model and year. Forty-two, forty-five, forty-eight. My mechanic friend said the tyres needed changing too. Suddenly sixty looked silly. I went back the next day and said, "Similar ones are around forty-five, and the tyres need work." We settled at forty-four. So that's how Minakshi, a girl who knew nothing about scooters, didn't pay sixty.

qa.q: What did the seller first say the scooter cost?
qa.a: "Sixty thousand, fixed."

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling when she almost said fifty-five?
qa.a: She felt pulled toward the seller's number, briefly pleased that fifty-five seemed like a steal, before she paused and felt unsure what it was really worth.

qa.q: Which steps helped Minakshi decide on her own terms?
qa.a: She asked what she'd think without the first number, then gathered three independent listings and a mechanic's view before going back.

qa.q: How might the seller have seen Minakshi's return with listings?
qa.a: The seller may have felt surprised and a bit cornered, realising she now had her own comparisons.

grounding: It shows a wise buyer who asks what she would judge without the first figure and gathers independent comparisons before deciding.

passage: I've shared a desk with Lavanya in the events team for a year, and last week I watched her do something I've now copied. A catering vendor quoted two lakh rupees for the annual function. Our manager said, "Try to get it to one-eighty." Everyone nodded. Lavanya didn't. She said, "Give me a day." I saw her sitting with a notepad, not looking at the quote at all. She told me later she'd asked herself: if I'd never seen two lakh, what would I expect for three hundred people? Then she called two other caterers and checked last year's bill. The next morning she walked into the manager's office with three numbers: one-forty, one-fifty-five, and last year's one-thirty. The vendor came down to one-fifty. I don't know if she was nervous. She seemed calm. I'm Lakshmi, and I now keep a notepad too.

qa.q: How many other caterers did Lavanya call?
qa.a: Two other caterers.

qa.q: How does Lakshmi seem to feel about what Lavanya did?
qa.a: Lakshmi seems impressed and a bit inspired, enough to start keeping a notepad too.

qa.q: What was wise about Lavanya's process?
qa.a: She set the first quote aside, asked what she'd expect without it, and gathered independent comparisons before negotiating.

qa.q: How might the manager have seen Lavanya's three numbers?
qa.a: The manager may have felt surprised and pleased that she brought a better target than one-eighty.

grounding: It shows, through a colleague's eyes, a wise decider who asks what she would judge without the first figure and gathers comparisons first.

passage:
A Monday in October. Anjali visited the first wedding hall for her sister's reception in Indore. The manager said, "Three lakh for the evening." Anjali felt the number settle in her head like a stone. Anything under three would feel cheap now. She caught herself and wrote in her phone: What would I think this is worth if I'd never heard three lakh?

That Thursday. With her friend Nirmala, she visited two more halls and called a third. Two lakh, two-twenty, two-forty. Nirmala added the cost her cousin had paid last year. The numbers told a different story.

The next Monday. Anjali went back to the first hall with her list. "The others are between two and two-forty." The manager hesitated, then offered two-thirty. Anjali said she'd decide after comparing the food menus too. Walking out, Nirmala grinned. "You didn't even blink at three."

qa.q: How much did the first wedding hall quote?
qa.a: Three lakh for the evening.

qa.q: How did Anjali feel when she heard three lakh, and what did she do with that feeling?
qa.a: She felt the number settle like a stone, sensing anything below would feel cheap, and she caught that feeling and wrote a question to reset her thinking.

qa.q: What made Anjali's decision stronger?
qa.a: Asking what she'd judge without the first figure, then collecting three other quotes and a past cost before deciding.

qa.q: How does Nirmala see Anjali's approach?
qa.a: Nirmala seems amused and proud, noticing Anjali wasn't pulled by the first number.

grounding: It shows a wise decider who asks what she'd judge without the first figure and gathers independent comparisons before deciding, over several days.

passage: At the primary school in Mysuru, a brown dog slept every afternoon under the neem tree by the gate. On Monday, Tushar's classmate told the class a long story about his cousin's dog bite: blood, a hospital, injections in the stomach. Tushar listened with wide eyes. On Tuesday, he refused to walk past the neem tree. He waited inside the gate until Rekha ma'am came. "All dogs bite," he said. "They're all dangerous." Rekha ma'am said, "Tushar, this dog has slept here for two years. Has it ever bitten anyone?" Tushar thought. No. He had even patted it once. But the cousin's story felt bigger. "It could," he said, and stamped his foot, angry that she didn't believe him. Rekha ma'am walked him past the tree, holding his hand. The dog didn't even open its eyes.

qa.q: Where did the brown dog sleep every afternoon?
qa.a: Under the neem tree by the gate.

qa.q: Why did Tushar feel so sure all dogs are dangerous?
qa.a: The vivid bite story felt huge and scary, so it seemed like what dogs usually do, and he felt afraid and angry that Rekha ma'am doubted him.

qa.q: How could Rekha ma'am help Tushar see the dog more fairly?
qa.a: She could remind him how many days he's walked past safely, and let him watch the dog calmly from a distance each day.

qa.q: How might Rekha ma'am feel when Tushar stamps his foot?
qa.a: Rekha ma'am likely feels patient and understanding, knowing the fear came from the story.

grounding: It shows a child who decides all dogs are dangerous after one vivid bite story, treating the most memorable case as the most common.

passage:
Sunday. At a cousin's birthday in Kolkata, an uncle told a loud story about a street dog biting a boy on the leg. Abhinav, seven, sat very still.

Wednesday. On the walk to school, Abhinav clutched his sister Lavanya's hand and pulled her across the road whenever he saw a dog, even old Bhola from their lane. "All dogs bite. Uncle said." When she tried to let go, he got angry and shouted.

Saturday. Lavanya counted with him. "How many dogs did we pass this week?" They counted on fingers. Twenty-two. "How many bit anyone?" Abhinav was quiet. "None." "And how many stories did you hear?" "One." He looked at Bhola, lying in the sun. He still held her hand tight, but he didn't pull her across the road.

qa.q: How many dogs did Abhinav and Lavanya count that week?
qa.a: Twenty-two.

qa.q: Why did Abhinav feel sure that all dogs bite?
qa.a: The uncle's vivid story stuck, so it felt like the usual thing, making him scared and angry when Lavanya tried to let go.

qa.q: What did Lavanya's counting help Abhinav see?
qa.a: It showed that twenty-two dogs passed without biting and only one story existed, helping him compare the vivid case to real life.

qa.q: How might Bhola seem to Lavanya compared with how Abhinav saw him?
qa.a: To Lavanya, Bhola is just the harmless old dog from their lane, lying in the sun; to Abhinav, after the story, he seemed like a danger.

grounding: It shows a child who decides all dogs are dangerous after one vivid story, until counting real encounters helps, over several days.

passage: Pranav, scared of the neighbour's dog after your friend's story? When I was a boy of eight, in Shillong, the tea-shop man told a story about a mad dog biting a boy, with snarling and running and crying. After that, I was sure every dog in the world wanted to bite me. Even our neighbour's old dog, Kalu, who slept on our doorstep. I shouted at my mother when she asked me to buy bread. One day she sat with me and said, "Anirban, how many times has Kalu bitten you?" "Never." "How many dogs have bitten anyone you know?" "Only the one in the story." She let me sit with Kalu, just touching his ear. Slowly, I remembered he was my friend.

qa.q: What was the name of the neighbour's old dog?
qa.a: Kalu.

qa.q: Why did young Anirban feel every dog wanted to bite him?
qa.a: The vivid tea-shop story felt so real that it seemed common, making him scared and angry enough to shout at his mother.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Anirban?
qa.a: His mother asked how often Kalu or any dog had actually bitten anyone, and then let him touch Kalu's ear, helping real experience outweigh the story.

qa.q: How might Anirban's mother have felt when he shouted about the bread?
qa.a: She probably felt worried and patient, realising the story had frightened him.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, as a child, one vivid dog-bite story made all dogs seem dangerous.

passage:
"Gautam bhaiya, I'm not going on the train to Pune."
"Jaya, it's a three-hour ride. You've done it ten times."
"Did you see the clip? The one where the train stopped and everyone was screaming?"
"That was in another country."
"There's another one every day on my feed. Bus crashes, bridge collapses, everything."
"How many times has the Pune train crashed?"
"I don't know. But I see accidents all the time."
"You see them all the time because the app keeps showing them to you. You watched one, it sent twenty."
Jaya hugged her knees. "It still feels like it'll happen."
"I know. Let's look it up. How many people take that train every day, and how many accidents in ten years?"
"...Fine. But if the number's scary, I'm not going."

qa.a: A three-hour ride.

qa.q: Why does the train feel dangerous to Jaya?
qa.a: She keeps seeing accident clips on her feed, so accidents feel frequent and she feels scared, even though it's a ride she's done ten times.

qa.q: What does Gautam bhaiya suggest, and why might it help?
qa.a: He suggests looking up how many people take the train and how many accidents happened, so real numbers can replace the feed's picture.

qa.q: How does Gautam bhaiya seem to see Jaya's fear?
qa.a: He seems patient and a bit worried, understanding it's the feed shaping her view and wanting to help calmly.

grounding: It shows a teenager who sees so many viral accident clips that ordinary travel feels far riskier than it is.

passage: In Class 9, I stopped cycling to school. I told my parents it was because of the sun. The real reason was the reels. Every night I scrolled through videos of road accidents: a scooter flipping, a truck swerving, a cyclist on a highway. After a while my feed was nothing but crashes. I became sure the roads of Nashik were a war zone. My friend Damini, who cycled with me every day for two years, kept asking why. I said, "Don't you watch the news?" She said, "Irawati, we've done this route five hundred times. Nothing happened." I didn't listen. I took the auto, which was actually more crowded and honestly more scary. Looking back, I think I mixed up how often I saw accidents with how often they happened.

qa.q: What did Irawati take instead of cycling?
qa.a: The auto.

qa.q: Why did the roads feel like a war zone to Irawati?
qa.a: Watching crash videos every night made accidents feel constant, so Irawati felt scared even though the real route had been safe for years.

qa.q: What could Irawati have done to check the fear?
qa.a: Irawati could have compared the five hundred safe rides with the videos, or looked up real local accident figures with a parent.

qa.q: How might Damini have felt cycling alone after Irawati stopped?
qa.a: Damini may have felt lonely and puzzled, missing a cycling friend and not understanding the fear.

grounding: It shows a teenager whose feed of accident videos made the city feel far riskier than it was, mistaking exposure for real frequency.

passage:
Class 10 counsellor's note, Thursday

Jyoti came to see me today because she wants to skip the school's bus trip to the science museum next week. She said, "Buses crash all the time. I see it every day." When I asked where, she showed me her phone: clip after clip of bus accidents, most from other countries, some years old.

She was clearly frightened, her hands cold. I didn't laugh or argue. I asked her how many school trips she'd been on. About twelve. How many had problems? None. Then we looked together at how the app decides what to show her. She was surprised that watching one crash had filled her feed.

She has agreed to think about going and to take a break from those videos this week. I'll check in with her on Monday.

— Jagdish

qa.q: How many school trips had Jyoti been on?
qa.a: About twelve.

qa.q: Why was Jyoti so frightened of the bus trip?
qa.a: Seeing crash clips every day made bus accidents feel constant, so she felt frightened even though her real trips had been safe.

qa.q: What did Jagdish do that helped Jyoti?
qa.a: Jagdish stayed calm, compared her real trips with the clips, and showed her how the app fills the feed, helping her see exposure isn't real frequency.

qa.q: How might Jyoti's friends see her wanting to skip the trip?
qa.a: Her friends might be confused or disappointed, not knowing the videos had made her so scared.

grounding: It shows, through a counsellor's note, a teenager whose feed of crash clips makes bus travel seem far riskier than it is.

passage: Dolma had cancelled her flight home to Gangtok for the holidays. After the news showed a crash abroad for three days straight, with shaky phone videos and crying relatives, she couldn't imagine getting on a plane. "I'll take the bus and train," she told her roommate. "Thirty hours, but safe." That evening Lalit, her friend from class, offered her a lift to the market on his scooter. He had only one helmet. "You wear it," she said, laughing, and hopped on the back without one. They zipped through Delhi traffic, weaving between buses. At a red light, Lalit turned. "You won't fly, but you'll ride without a helmet?" "It's just the market," Dolma said. It didn't feel dangerous at all. The crash videos did.

qa.q: How long did Dolma say the bus and train journey would take?
qa.a: Thirty hours.

qa.q: Why did flying feel more dangerous to Dolma than riding without a helmet?
qa.a: The dramatic crash coverage made flying feel terrifying, while the scooter ride felt ordinary and safe, so she felt calm on it despite the real risk.

qa.q: What would you advise Dolma?
qa.a: Wear a helmet every time, or take an auto if there's only one, and look at real figures for flying before deciding it's too risky.

qa.q: How does Lalit see Dolma's choices?
qa.a: Lalit seems puzzled and a bit worried, noticing she fears the rare danger but ignores the common one.

grounding: It shows a student who fears flying after dramatic coverage but rides a scooter without a helmet, as memorable dangers crowd out common ones.

passage:
"Binita, why are you wearing a mask on the terrace?"
"Akash, didn't you see the news? That rare virus. They showed a whole family in hospital."

passage: In my second year of college, I was terrified of a rare brain infection. A news channel ran a special about it for a week, with dramatic music and a young student in a hospital bed. I washed my hands constantly and avoided swimming pools. But every evening, I rode pillion on Bhupen's scooter to the tea stall, no helmet, hair flying. I didn't even think about it. One night a car swerved and we nearly hit the divider. My heart was in my mouth. Bhupen said, shaken, "We need helmets." I realised I'd spent a week scared of something I'd probably never meet, and zero minutes scared of the thing that almost happened. Now I wear a helmet every time. And I check how common a danger is before I panic. That's Ganga's lesson from second year.

qa.q: Where did Ganga ride pillion every evening?
qa.a: On Bhupen's scooter to the tea stall.

qa.q: Why did the rare infection feel scarier than riding without a helmet?
qa.a: The week of dramatic news made the infection vivid and terrifying, while the scooter ride felt routine, so Ganga felt no fear on it until the near miss.

qa.q: What changed for Ganga after the near miss?
qa.a: Ganga now wears a helmet every time and checks how common a danger is before panicking.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have felt after the car swerved?
qa.a: Bhupen felt shaken and frightened, and likely guilty for riding without helmets.

grounding: It shows a student who feared a rare illness after dramatic coverage but rode without a helmet, as the memorable danger crowded out the common one.

passage: I became a father in March, and by May I noticed something in our family group chat. Every day, someone forwarded a message: a child kidnapped from a park, men in a white van, a video from somewhere unnamed. My aunt called Bidisha, my wife, in a panic. "Don't take the baby out!" Everyone was frightened. Meanwhile, at home, the same aunt had left her medicine box on the low table, and the balcony grill had a gap wide enough for a crawling baby. Nobody mentioned those. I felt uneasy, and a bit angry. So I looked up the police figures for our city. Kidnappings by strangers were very rare; most messages were old or false. Falls at home were far more common. I told the group, gently. Then I moved the medicine box to a high shelf and called a welder about the grill. I'm Jeevan, and I'm learning which worries to keep.

qa.q: What did the family group chat keep forwarding?
qa.a: Messages about a child kidnapped from a park and men in a white van.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel noticing the panic over forwards but not the home risks?
qa.a: Jeevan felt uneasy and a bit angry, seeing real everyday dangers ignored while a rare, vivid threat caused panic.

qa.q: What steps did Jeevan take, and why were they wise?
qa.a: He checked the actual police figures, shared them gently, moved the medicine box high and called a welder for the balcony gap, focusing on the common risks.

qa.q: How might Jeevan's aunt see the forwarded messages?
qa.a: His aunt seems genuinely frightened, believing the messages show a real and common danger.

grounding: It shows a new father noticing relatives panic over a kidnapping rumour while ignoring everyday home risks, and asking what the numbers say.

passage:
A Tuesday in July. Omkar's mother-in-law arrived at their Mumbai flat, clutching her phone. "A child was stolen from a hospital! It's on every group!" Leela, holding their two-month-old, went pale. Omkar watched the fear spread through the room.

That Friday. His mother-in-law now wouldn't let anyone take the baby to the building garden. But she kept leaving the hot iron on the edge of the bed, the cord dangling. Omkar noticed. He also noticed the kitchen floor wet and slippery near the baby's mat. He asked quietly, "Has anyone checked if this story is true? How often does this happen?"

The next Monday. Omkar had looked up the numbers. The story was two years old, from another state. He showed Leela and her mother. Then he said, "What scares me more is the iron." He fixed a hook for it on the wall. His mother-in-law, a little embarrassed, started unplugging it after use.

qa.q: Where was the child said to be stolen from?
qa.a: From a hospital.

qa.q: How did Omkar feel watching the fear spread?
qa.a: Omkar felt concerned and a bit detached, noticing the panic about a rumour while real home dangers went unseen.

qa.q: Which steps did Omkar take to protect the baby?
qa.a: He checked the facts on the rumour, pointed out the hanging iron, and fixed a hook for it, focusing on real everyday risks.

qa.q: How might Omkar's mother-in-law feel once she learns the story was old?
qa.a: She seems a little embarrassed but relieved, and starts unplugging the iron after use.

grounding: It shows a new father noticing relatives panic over a forwarded kidnapping rumour while ignoring home risks, and asking what the numbers say, over several days.

passage: Pankaj, the family group is sending you kidnapping videos? Let me tell you what happened when your cousin was born. I was twenty-five, a new father in Guwahati. My uncles forwarded messages every day: kidnappers in white vans, children stolen from parks. My mother cried on the phone. She wanted the baby locked inside. I was scared too. But I noticed our house had a pond in the back with no fence, and the stairs had no railing. Nobody in the family talked about those. So I went to the police station and asked the officer: how many kidnappings here, really? He laughed and said almost none, and those were mostly family disputes. But drownings in small ponds, he said, happen every monsoon. I came home and built a fence that week. That's what Mridul learned: ask what the numbers say, then fix the real dangers.

qa.q: What did the police officer say happens every monsoon?

qa.q: How did young Mridul feel when the kidnapping messages came?
qa.a: Mridul felt scared too, but also uneasy, noticing that real dangers like the unfenced pond were being ignored.

qa.a: His mother felt frightened and tearful, believing the messages meant the baby was in constant danger.

passage: Last winter a friend sent me a long article about a hostel fire in another city. The photos were awful: blackened stairs, a girl's shoe on the pavement. That night I lay awake in my own working women's hostel, staring at the ceiling, planning to move out. I was really scared. In the morning, I made myself pause. How often does this actually happen? I looked up the fire department's yearly report. Hostel fires were rare, and most happened where exits were blocked. So I didn't move. Instead, I checked our fire exits, found one locked, and told the warden, who opened it that day. My friend Tanuja said I was brave to stay. I don't think it was bravery. I just asked a question before letting one story decide for me. I'm Uma.

qa.q: What did Uma find on checking the fire exits?
qa.a: One was locked.

qa.q: How did Uma feel on the night of reading the article?
qa.a: Uma felt really scared, lying awake and planning to move out after seeing the vivid photos.

qa.q: What did Uma do instead of moving out, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Uma checked the fire department's report, learned such fires are rare and linked to blocked exits, then checked and fixed the locked exit.

qa.q: How does Tanuja see Uma's choice to stay?
qa.a: Tanuja sees it as brave, though Uma thinks it was just checking the facts.

grounding: It shows a mature person who pauses when a vivid story scares her, checks reliable figures and acts sensibly instead of changing her habits from fear.

passage:
Supervisor's note, Friday

Sharmila, our senior lab assistant, came in on Monday shaken. Her neighbour had told her a vivid story about someone who got a serious infection from a small cut in a lab. Sharmila had been thinking of asking for a transfer to the office side.

I was impressed by what she did next. She told me, "Before I decide, I want to know how often this really happens." She checked the safety records for our institute and the national lab safety guidelines. Serious infections were very rare, and almost always linked to missing gloves or broken protocols.

She stayed in the lab. She did ask for a refresher on the glove and first-aid protocol for the whole team, which we ran on Thursday.

I've asked her to share how she thought it through at our next meeting.

— Alka

qa.q: What did Sharmila want to know before deciding?
qa.a: How often this really happens.

qa.q: How was Sharmila feeling when she came in on Monday?
qa.a: She felt shaken and frightened after the neighbour's vivid story, enough to consider a transfer.

qa.q: Why was Sharmila's approach a good one?
qa.a: She paused and checked reliable records before changing her job, then took a useful safety step instead of acting from fear alone.

qa.q: How does Alka see Sharmila's approach?
qa.a: Alka is impressed and wants Sharmila to share her thinking with the team.

grounding: It shows, through a supervisor's note, a mature person who pauses when a vivid story scares her and checks reliable figures before changing her habits.

passage:
Sunday night

Seema forwarded a video today about a woman who got terribly sick from street food. Vomiting, hospital, drip. I watched it twice and felt my stomach turn. I love the chaat stall near my office. I was ready to swear off it forever.

Then I stopped. I remembered what I promised myself after the dengue scare last year: check before panicking. How often does this happen? I looked up the city health department's page. Food poisoning happens, yes, but it's mostly linked to stalls without clean water or fridges. My chaat uncle has a filter and covers everything.

So I'm not giving it up. I'll keep watching for clean water and fresh food. And I told Seema what I found. She said, "Farida, you're so calm." Not calm. Just checking.

Farida

qa.q: What did Seema forward?
qa.a: A video about a woman who got terribly sick from street food.

qa.q: How did Farida feel watching the video?
qa.a: Farida felt a turning stomach and fear, ready to give up the chaat stall forever.

qa.q: What made Farida's final decision a sensible one?
qa.a: Checking the health department's information showed the real risk depended on clean water and fresh food, so Farida kept going while watching for those signs.

qa.q: How might Seema see Farida's reaction?
qa.a: Seema sees Farida as calm, perhaps a little surprised that Farida didn't panic.

grounding: It shows a mature person who pauses when a vivid story feels frightening and checks reliable information before changing habits.

passage:
"Farida didi, the new boy in my class is going to be the topper."
"Which one, Kamal?"
"The quiet one with thick glasses. He looks like a topper."
"How do you know he's clever?"
"He wears glasses. And he doesn't talk."
"Hmm. And the other new boy?"
"Mohan? He's always shouting and joking. He'll probably fail."
"Did you see their marks?"
"No. But you can tell."
A week later.
"Didi! Didi! Guess what?"
"What?"
"Mohan got the highest in maths! And the glasses boy got less than me!"
"But you said you could tell."
Kamal scratched his head. "I thought I could."

qa.q: Who got the highest in maths?
qa.a: Mohan.

qa.q: Why did Kamal feel sure the quiet boy would be the topper?
qa.a: Glasses and silence matched Kamal's idea of a clever student, so it felt like proof, and he was surprised when it wasn't true.

qa.q: What could Kamal do next time he meets someone new?
qa.a: He could wait to see what they actually do in class, like their answers and marks, before deciding how clever they are.

qa.q: How might Mohan feel if he knew Kamal expected him to fail?
qa.a: Mohan might feel hurt or annoyed at being judged for being loud.

grounding: It shows a child who assumes the quiet boy with glasses is clever and the loud boy is weak, until real marks prove otherwise.

passage: In Class 4, when two new boys joined, I was sure I knew all about them from one look. Jeetu wore glasses and sat quietly at the front. I thought, he's the topper type. Bunty sat at the back, laughing loudly and drumming on the desk. I thought, he'll get zero. I even told my friends. Then Urmila ma'am gave a surprise test. Bunty got full marks. Jeetu got six out of ten. I was so surprised that I asked Urmila ma'am if she'd mixed up the papers. She laughed and said, "Omkar, you can't see a brain through glasses." I felt a bit silly. After that, I started waiting to see what people did before deciding.

qa.q: How many marks did Jeetu get in the surprise test?
qa.a: Six out of ten.

qa.q: Why was Omkar so sure about Jeetu and Bunty at first?
qa.a: The glasses and quietness matched Omkar's picture of a topper, and the laughing matched a weak student, so it felt certain, and later Omkar felt surprised and silly.

qa.q: What did Omkar change after the test?
qa.a: Omkar started waiting to see what people actually did before deciding what they were like.

qa.q: How might Urmila ma'am have felt when Omkar asked if she mixed up the papers?
qa.a: Urmila ma'am seemed amused and used the moment to teach gently.

grounding: It shows a child who judges two new classmates by their look and manner, until test results show appearance isn't evidence.

passage:
Class 3 note, Tuesday

During group work today, Karthik refused to be in a group with Rohit. "He's loud and messy. He'll be bad at maths." He wanted Arun instead, "because Arun wears glasses and is quiet, so he's clever."

I let the groups stay mixed. In the maths game, Rohit solved the puzzle first, shouting with excitement. Arun got stuck and asked Karthik for help.

After class, Karthik came up to me looking confused. "Ma'am, Rohit is good at maths?" I asked him how he had decided before. He said, "He looked like he wouldn't be." I told him that the best way to know is to see what someone does.

I'll keep mixing groups this week.

— Ankita

qa.q: Who solved the puzzle first in the maths game?
qa.a: Rohit.

qa.q: Why did Karthik feel so sure Arun was clever?
qa.a: Arun's glasses and quietness matched Karthik's idea of a clever child, so it felt like proof, and later he felt confused and surprised.

qa.q: What was wise about Ankita's decision to keep groups mixed?
qa.a: It let Karthik see real evidence of what each child could do, which is better than telling him he was wrong.

qa.q: How might Rohit feel if he knew why Karthik didn't want him in the group?
qa.a: Rohit might feel hurt at being judged as bad at maths for being loud.

grounding: It shows, through a teacher's note, a child who assumes a quiet boy with glasses is clever and a loud boy weak, until he sees real evidence.

passage:
Dear Baljeet,

New school update. On the first day, I decided who everyone was. The tall boy with the basketball shoes: sports captain, bad at studies. The girl who speaks softly in Tamil-accented English: maths genius. The guy with the earring and the loud laugh: trouble, stay away.

Guess what? Three weeks later, the tall boy tops in chemistry and can't even dribble. The soft-spoken girl hates maths and runs the drama club. And the earring guy, Rizwan, is the one who helped me find the library and lent me his notes when I was sick.

I felt so sure on day one. It really felt like I could tell just by looking. Now I feel a bit embarrassed. I wonder how many people I've guessed wrong before.

Write back soon.

Farhan

qa.q: Who lent Farhan notes when Farhan was sick?
qa.a: Rizwan, the earring guy.

qa.q: Why did Farhan feel so sure on the first day?
qa.a: Each person seemed to match a familiar type, so the match felt like proof; now Farhan feels surprised and a bit embarrassed.

qa.q: What could Farhan do differently with the next new people?
qa.a: Farhan could hold first guesses loosely and wait to see what people actually do before deciding who they are.

qa.q: How might Rizwan feel if he knew Farhan first thought he was trouble?
qa.a: Rizwan might feel hurt or amused, having been kind despite the unfair first judgement.

grounding: It shows a teenager who judges classmates' abilities from how they look or speak and is surprised when reality disagrees.

passage: Nitin, you asked why I changed seats in maths class. Okay, so here's the story. When I joined the new school in Class 9, I sat next to the boy who wore thick glasses and carried three geometry boxes. I thought, this guy's obviously a maths genius, I'll learn from him. And I avoided the boy from the hockey team who always joked around, because I thought, sports types don't do maths. Then the first test came. Glasses boy got thirty-five out of a hundred. Hockey boy, Joel, got ninety-eight. I literally stared at the list for a whole minute. I was so surprised. It felt like my brain had lied to me. So I asked Joel if I could sit with him. He laughed and said, "You thought I was dumb, didn't you?" I said sorry. Now he explains trigonometry better than the teacher. That's Vaibhav's lesson.

qa.q: What did the hockey boy score in the first test?
qa.a: Ninety-eight.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav feel sure about the glasses boy and the hockey boy?
qa.a: Each matched a familiar type, so it felt obvious, and the results left Vaibhav very surprised, as if the brain had lied.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav do after seeing the results, and why was it good?
qa.a: Vaibhav apologised to Joel and asked to sit with him, choosing based on real evidence instead of looks.

qa.q: How did Joel seem to react when Vaibhav asked to sit with him?
qa.a: Joel seemed amused and guessed the unfair judgement, but was generous enough to help anyway.

grounding: It shows a teenager who decides who is good at maths from how people look and is surprised when reality disagrees.

passage:
June, first week. Shalini joined Imran's Class 11 in Lucknow from a village school. She wore oiled plaits and spoke Hindi with a rural accent. Imran decided at once: she'd be weak at science. When the teacher paired them for the physics project, he groaned. "She won't know anything."

July, a Wednesday. During the project, Shalini quietly corrected Imran's circuit diagram. He thought it was luck. She explained why his resistor was in the wrong place. He said nothing.

August, a Monday. The first term results went up. Shalini topped physics. Imran stood in front of the board, cheeks hot. He thought about the groan, the look he had given her. He went to find her. "Your diagram was right. I was... I thought you wouldn't know." Shalini smiled a little. "People always think that." Imran felt a sting of surprise at how many times she must have heard it.

qa.q: Where did Shalini come from?
qa.a: A village school.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when he saw Shalini top physics?
qa.a: Imran felt surprised and embarrassed, cheeks hot, as he realised how unfair his first judgement had been.

qa.q: What could Imran do to avoid such snap judgements?
qa.a: He could notice when someone's look or accent triggers a guess, and wait for real evidence like their work before deciding.

qa.q: What is it like for Shalini to be underestimated?
qa.a: Shalini seems used to it, saying 'people always think that', which suggests she has faced this judgement many times.

grounding: It shows a teenager who judges a classmate's science ability by her accent and appearance, and is surprised when reality disagrees, over several months.

passage: In Helsinki, the university business course split into project teams, and Ulla's group had to choose a leader. Mikko spoke first, fluent and confident, with slides already in his head. "I've got this." Ulla voted for him at once. He looked like a leader. Sami, who rarely spoke, had quietly finished every reading and sent the group a clear task list the night before. Ulla hadn't even opened it. Over three weeks, Mikko kept giving great speeches in meetings but missed deadlines. Sami kept doing the work, fixing the spreadsheets at midnight. At the final presentation, Mikko froze on a question about numbers. Sami answered it calmly. Walking out, Ulla felt a bit ashamed. She had picked the voice, not the work.

qa.q: Who sent the group a clear task list the night before?
qa.a: Sami.

qa.q: Why did Ulla vote for Mikko so quickly?
qa.a: Mikko's fluent, confident style matched her picture of a leader, so it felt like competence, and later she felt a bit ashamed of that choice.

qa.q: What could Ulla look at next time the group picks a leader?
qa.a: She could look at who actually does the work, like Sami's task list and finished readings, before being swayed by confident talk.

qa.q: How might Sami have felt when the group chose Mikko?
qa.a: Sami may have felt overlooked but carried on doing the work quietly.

grounding: It shows a student who picks a confident speaker as project leader and overlooks a quieter, more reliable teammate, mistaking style for competence.

passage: The college fest committee met in the seminar hall, and Tanuja had to pick a head for the sponsorship team. Eshaan stood up and gave a speech about "vision" and "big brands" with perfect English and a smile. The room clapped. Tanuja felt sure: he was the one. Rukmini, from second year, sat at the back. Last year she had quietly got four local shops to sponsor the music night, but nobody remembered because she never talked about it. Tanuja chose Eshaan. By the second week, Eshaan had made three presentations and zero calls. Rukmini, on her own, had two shopkeepers ready to sign. Tanuja saw the list and felt her face go warm. She'd been dazzled by how Eshaan spoke, not by what either of them had done.

qa.q: How many local shops had Rukmini got to sponsor the music night last year?
qa.a: Four local shops.

qa.q: Why did Eshaan feel like the right choice to Tanuja?
qa.a: His fluent, confident speech felt like proof of ability, so Tanuja felt sure, and later embarrassed at being dazzled by style.

qa.q: What would you advise Tanuja for choosing leads in future?
qa.a: Look at past results, like Rukmini's sponsorships, before listening to speeches, and ask each person what they've actually done.

qa.q: How might Rukmini feel about being overlooked?
qa.a: Rukmini may feel unnoticed and a bit hurt, but she keeps working quietly.

grounding: It shows a student who picks a fluent speaker as team head and overlooks a quieter, more reliable member, mistaking style for competence.

passage:
Dear Anirban,

Remember the robotics project last term, when I chose Kunal as team lead over you? I owe you a letter.

Kunal talked like a CEO. He had the jargon, the posture, the "let's crush this" energy. You barely spoke in meetings, just nodded and took notes. I thought: Kunal will make us win.

Then Kunal missed two deadlines, and you stayed up three nights fixing the motor code he had promised to write. At the competition, it was your code that worked. I didn't even say thank you properly.

I think I mistook confidence for competence. It's embarrassing to admit. You were the reliable one all along, and I didn't see it because you were quiet.

Next project, I'd like you to lead, if you're willing.

Amandeep

qa.q: How many nights did Anirban stay up fixing the motor code?
qa.a: Three nights.

qa.q: Why does Amandeep feel embarrassed about choosing Kunal?
qa.a: Amandeep realises the choice was based on Kunal's confident style rather than real work, and feels embarrassed for overlooking the reliable teammate.

qa.q: What is Amandeep doing to fix the mistake?
qa.a: Amandeep admits the error, thanks Anirban and asks Anirban to lead next time, based on what Anirban actually did.

qa.q: How might Anirban feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Anirban may feel surprised, touched and finally recognised for the quiet work.

grounding: It shows a student who chose a confident speaker as project leader and overlooked a quieter, more reliable teammate, mistaking style for competence.

passage: I've been hiring manager at a small design studio in Pune for two years, and last month I noticed something about my co-panellist, Sudha. We were interviewing for junior designers. Sudha lit up at every candidate from the same design school our best designer came from. "She reminds me of Pooja," she said twice. She rated them high before looking at their portfolios. A candidate from a small college in Nagpur brought an excellent portfolio. Sudha said, "Hmm, not really our type." I felt uneasy. We were judging resemblance, not work. After the interviews, I proposed a simple scoring sheet: portfolio, problem-solving task, and interview answers, each scored separately, before we discussed. Sudha agreed, a bit stiffly. With the sheet, the Nagpur candidate came out top. I'm Darshan, and as a man who once got hired for 'looking right,' I should have noticed sooner.

qa.q: What did Sudha say about the candidate from Nagpur?
qa.a: "Hmm, not really our type."

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling as Sudha rated candidates by resemblance?
qa.a: Darshan felt uneasy, realising they were judging people by how much they looked like past successes rather than their actual work.

qa.q: Why does structured scoring help, as Darshan proposed?
qa.a: Scoring portfolio, task and answers separately before discussing makes each candidate judged on evidence, not on resemblance to someone else.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel about the scoring sheet?
qa.a: Sudha seems a bit stiff and perhaps defensive, but agrees to try it.

grounding: It shows a hiring manager who notices a panel favouring candidates who resemble earlier successes and proposes structured scoring based on evidence.

passage:
A Monday in February. On the interview panel for sales trainees in Bengaluru, Yash noticed that Rehana, his co-panellist, smiled most at tall, confident men from engineering colleges, just like their current top salesman. "He's a natural," she said after five minutes with one of them.

That Thursday. The candidates she liked had weaker answers to the customer scenario. A quiet woman from a commerce college had the best solution but got a low mark from Rehana. "She's not the sales type." Yash felt his jaw tighten. He wasn't sure how to raise it without sounding like an accusation.

The next Monday. Yash brought a scoring sheet to the panel: scenario answer, product knowledge, and a role-play, each scored alone, before any discussion. "It'll make us fairer," he said. Rehana shrugged but used it. The quiet woman scored highest. Rehana looked at the sheet for a long time.

qa.q: Who did Rehana say was 'a natural'?
qa.a: One of the tall, confident men from engineering colleges.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling when Rehana dismissed the best solution?
qa.a: Yash felt frustrated, his jaw tightening, and unsure how to raise it without sounding like an accusation.

qa.q: What did Yash's scoring sheet change, and why?
qa.a: It made each candidate scored on answers, knowledge and role-play separately, so the quiet woman's real ability showed instead of resemblance to the top salesman.

qa.q: How might Rehana feel looking at the final scores?
qa.a: Rehana may feel surprised and thoughtful, seeing that her first impressions didn't match the evidence.

grounding: It shows a manager who notices a panel favouring candidates who look like earlier successes and brings in structured scoring, over a week.

passage: Afreen, you're joining your first interview panel next week? Let me tell you what I saw as a young man of twenty-five, a junior manager in a bank in Kolkata. Our branch head liked candidates who looked like him: Bengali, from his college, played cricket. He'd say, "This one has spark," in the first minute. I noticed that a quiet young woman from Siliguri with top scores was rejected because she "didn't fit." It bothered me for weeks. I was nervous, being junior. But I went to him with a simple idea: let's each score candidates on the same questions, separately, then compare. He grumbled but agreed to try it for one round. That round, two people from outside his usual type came out on top, and both became excellent officers. So, Afreen, use a scoring sheet. It's how Pranav learned to see people, not types.

qa.q: What did Pranav propose to the branch head?
qa.a: That they each score candidates on the same questions, separately, then compare.

qa.q: How did young Pranav feel about the Siliguri candidate's rejection?
qa.a: Pranav felt bothered for weeks and nervous, being junior, about raising the unfairness with the branch head.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the hiring fairer?
qa.a: Pranav's decision to suggest separate scoring on the same questions, which let candidates outside the usual type be judged on evidence.

qa.q: How might the branch head have seen the new scoring at first?
qa.a: The branch head grumbled, perhaps feeling his judgement was questioned, but agreed to try it.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how he noticed a panel favouring candidates who resembled earlier successes and proposed structured scoring.
